paper.title_en: First strength measurements of low-energy resonances in the <math><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>Sc</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>45</mn></mmultiscripts><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>)</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>Ti</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>46</mn></mmultiscripts></mrow></math> reaction and its astrophysical implications
paper.abstract_en: The <math><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>Sc</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>45</mn></mmultiscripts><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>)</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>Ti</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>46</mn></mmultiscripts></mrow></math> reaction plays an important role in both hydrostatic and explosive nucleosynthesis. During hydrostatic oxygen and silicon burning in massive stars, including dynamic processes such as convective carbon-oxygen (C-O) shell mergers, it acts as a bottleneck that regulates the reaction flow in the Sc-Ti mass region. In oxygen-neon (ONe) novae, the ejecta indicate the production of elements up to the Fe group, as observed in V1974 Cygni, and the <math><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>Sc</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>45</mn></mmultiscripts><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>)</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>Ti</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>46</mn></mmultiscripts></mrow></math> reaction links nuclei above Ca to the Fe region. In core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe), it influences the production of the radioactive isotope <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Sc</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>47</mn></mmultiscripts></math>. At present, the thermonuclear reaction rate is based on statistical model calculations. In this work, we report on measurements of the <math><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>Sc</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>45</mn></mmultiscripts><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>)</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>Ti</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>46</mn></mmultiscripts></mrow></math> reaction performed using the 5 MV accelerator at the Nuclear Science Laboratory, University of Notre Dame, over a laboratory proton energy range of 526–1275 keV. We present the first direct measurements of the resonance strengths for six resonances at <math><mrow><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi>lab</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>917.4</mn></mrow></math>, 1026.0, 1031.1, 1049.7, 1059.4, and 1257.5 keV, together with integrated resonance strengths at <math><mrow><msup><mi>E</mi><mi>lab</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>555</mn></mrow></math>, 630, 700, 761, and 871 keV. For resonance energies below the lowest directly measured energy, available transfer-reaction data were used to estimate the resonance strengths. An updated thermonuclear reaction rate is derived, and its astrophysical implications are discussed.
